claim: Human flap endonuclease 1 (FEN1) and related structure-specific 5'nucleases precisely identify and incise aberrant DNA structures during replication, repair and recombination to avoid genomic instability.
source: Human flap endonuclease 1 (FEN1) and related structure-specific 5'nucleases precisely identify and incise aberrant DNA structures during replication, repair and recombination to avoid genomic instability.
evidence: This is a general statement about FEN1 function supported by established scientific knowledge in the field.

claim: Single-molecule sub-millisecond and millisecond analyses of FEN1 reveal a protein-DNA induced-fit mechanism that efficiently verifies substrate and suppresses off-target cleavage.
source: Here, single-molecule sub-millisecond and millisecond analyses of FEN1 reveal a protein-DNA induced-fit mechanism that efficiently verifies substrate and suppresses off-target cleavage.
evidence: This claim is supported by the single-molecule FRET experiments described throughout the manuscript.

claim: FEN1 sculpts DNA with diffusion-limited kinetics to test DNA substrate.
source: FEN1 sculpts DNA with diffusion-limited kinetics to test DNA substrate.
evidence: This is supported by the measured kon-bending rate of 1.4 ± 0.03×10^8 M^-1 s^-1 shown in Figure 1G.

claim: DNA distortion mutually 'locks' protein and DNA conformation and enables substrate verification with extreme precision.
source: This DNA distortion mutually 'locks' protein and DNA conformation and enables substrate verification with extreme precision.
evidence: This is supported by the single-molecule cleavage data showing FEN1 never misses cleavage of cognate substrate (Figure 2).

claim: FEN1 never misses cleavage of its cognate substrate.
source: Strikingly, FEN1 never misses cleavage of its cognate substrate while blocking probable formation of catalytically competent interactions with noncognate substrates and fostering their pre-incision dissociation.
evidence: This is directly demonstrated by single-molecule cleavage experiments showing every DNA bending event led to successful cleavage (Figure 2A).

claim: FEN1 blocks probable formation of catalytically competent interactions with noncognate substrates.
source: Strikingly, FEN1 never misses cleavage of its cognate substrate while blocking probable formation of catalytically competent interactions with noncognate substrates and fostering their pre-incision dissociation.
evidence: This is supported by data showing noncognate substrates undergo multiple cycles of bending without cleavage (Figure 5).

claim: 5'nucleases operate by uniformly binding to a bent junction to place the scissile phosphate near the active site.
source: This conserved cleavage site despite diverse structures operates by uniformly binding to a bent junction to place the scissile phosphate near the active site (Liu et al., 2015; Orans et al., 2011; Tsutakawa et al., 2011) (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by citations to structural studies and Figure 1B showing the bent DNA structure.

claim: Catalysis requires changes in the protein conformation that assembles the active site.
source: Catalysis is proposed to require changes in the protein conformation that assembles the active site (Devos et al., 2007; Lee et al., 2015; Liu et al., 2015; Orans et al., 2011; Sakurai et al., 2005; Tsutakawa et al., 2011) and movement of the scissile phosphate closer to the catalytic metals (Liu et al., 2015; Orans et al., 2011; Tsutakawa et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior structural and biochemical studies.

claim: FEN1 maintains exquisite specificity with extreme efficiency that enhances the hydrolysis rate of target phosphodiester bonds by ~10^17.
source: Strikingly, FEN1 maintains exquisite specificity with extreme efficiency that enhances the hydrolysis rate of target phosphodiester bonds by ~1017, and in vitro reaction rates resemble those of enzyme-substrate encounters (Finger et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior biochemical characterization.

claim: FEN1 recognizes dsDNA bearing a double-flap (DF) nick junction consisting of short ssDNA or ssRNA 5'flaps and strictly one nucleotide (nt) ssDNA 3'flap.
source: FEN1 recognizes dsDNA bearing a double-flap (DF) nick junction consisting of short ssDNA or ssRNA 5'flaps and strictly one nucleotide (nt) ssDNA 3'flap (Figure 1A) (Finger et al., 2009; Kao et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citations and illustrated in Figure 1A.

claim: DF intermediates are produced during Okazaki fragment synthesis on the lagging strand and during long-patch base excision repair.
source: DF intermediates are produced during Okazaki fragment synthesis on the lagging strand and during long-patch base excision repair (Garg et al., 2004; Liu et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior studies on DNA replication and repair.

claim: Mutations that reduce FEN1 expression or alter its activity are linked to cancers and genetic diseases.
source: Mutations that reduce FEN1 expression or alter its activity are linked to cancers and genetic diseases (Balakrishnan and Bambara, 2013; Henneke et al., 2003; Kucherlapati et al., 2002; Zheng et al., 2007, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to studies linking FEN1 to disease.

claim: FEN1 contacts duplex DNA from both sides of the flap junction through a 100° bend stabilized by the interaction of the superfamily-conserved hydrophobic wedge with the junction.
source: FEN1 contacts duplex DNA from both sides of the flap junction through a 100° bend stabilized by the interaction of the superfamily-conserved hydrophobic wedge with the junction (Figure 1B) (Tsutakawa et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to structural study and shown in Figure 1B.

claim: A superfamily-conserved helical gateway covered by a unique FEN1 helical cap forms a narrow cavity at the DNA junction suitable to select for threading ss 5'flaps with a free end.
source: A superfamily-conserved helical gateway covered by a unique FEN1 helical cap forms a narrow cavity at the DNA junction. This gateway is suitable to select for threading ss 5'flaps with a free end (Figure 1B) (Gloor et al., 2010; Patel et al., 2012; Sobhy et al., 2013; Tsutakawa et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to structural and functional studies and illustrated in Figure 1B.

claim: Part of the cap-helical gateway and the 3'flap-binding pocket appear disordered without DNA but ordered when bound to the 3'flap.
source: Part of the cap-helical gateway, which contains catalytically indispensable residues, and the 3'flap-binding pocket appear disordered without DNA (Sakurai et al., 2005), but it is ordered when bound to the 3'flap (Figure 1B) (Chapados et al., 2004; Tsutakawa et al., 2011), suggesting DNA-induced ordering of the cap-helical gateway.
evidence: This is supported by citations to structural studies and shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The scissile phosphate nucleotide is fully paired at the nick junction and away from the active site's metal ions in substrate complexes.
source: Comparison of substrate and product complexes shows that the scissile phosphate nucleotide is fully paired at the nick junction and away from the active site's metal ions, suggesting that unpairing flanking nucleotides may move ssDNA into the active site (Tsutakawa et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to structural comparison study.

claim: NonEQ DF-6,1 substrate alone shows a single FRET state with no transitions.
source: The single-molecule time traces of the substrate alone showed a single FRET state with no transition from this state (Figure 1D,E); FRET efficiency histograms generated from multiple single molecules fit to a single Gaussian (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A,B).
evidence: This is directly shown by the experimental data in Figure 1D, E and supplement figures.

claim: The conformer of the duplex arms of the substrate was insensitive to variation in the concentration of divalent metal ions (Mg2+).
source: The conformer of the duplex arms of the substrate was insensitive to variation in the concentration of divalent metal ions (Mg2+) (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A,B), type of metal ion (Mg2+ versus Ca2+) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A,B and Figure 1—figure supplement 2A,B) or 5'flap length (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A,B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data shown in the supplement figures.

claim: Extended DNA (~165°) was the most energetically favorable conformer in DF-6,1 according to MD simulations.
source: Potential mean force molecular dynamics (MD) simulations showed that extended DNA (~165°) was the most energetically favorable conformer in DF-6,1 (Figure 1F and Figure 1—figure supplement 3A,B).
evidence: This is supported by computational MD simulation data shown in Figure 1F.

claim: Base stacking at the nick junction and between the 3'flap base and the first base on the 5'flap stabilized the extended conformer.
source: Base stacking at the nick junction and between the 3'flap base and the first base on the 5'flap stabilized this extended conformer (Figure 1—figure supplement 3B).
evidence: This is supported by MD simulation analysis shown in the supplement figure.

claim: Adding FEN1 to DNA NonEQ DF-6,1 showed transitions to the bent states in a single step to form a stable FEN1−DNAbent complex.
source: In fact, adding FEN1 to DNA NonEQ DF-6,1 in both labeling schemes showed transitions to the bent states in a single step to form a stable FEN1−DNAbent complex that rarely dissociated during our 60 s standard acquisition time (Figure 1D,E).
evidence: This is directly demonstrated by single-molecule time traces shown in Figure 1D and E.

claim: The DNA bending dissociation constant (Kd-bending) was 3.9 ± 0.4 nM for NonEQ DF-6,1Flap and 4.6 ± 0.6 nM for NonEQ DF-6,1dsDNA.
source: We calculated the DNA bending dissociation constant (Kd-bending) from the FRET efficiency histogram-binding isotherm to be 3.9 ± 0.4 nM and 4.6 ± 0.6 nM for NonEQ DF-6,1Flap and NonEQ DF-6,1dsDNA, respectively (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A,B).
evidence: This is calculated from experimental FRET data shown in the supplement figures.

claim: The Kd-bending agreed with the nM range of Km from bulk cleavage assays.
source: This dissociation constant agreed with the nM range of Km from bulk cleavage assays (Figure 1—figure supplement 4A) (Finger et al., 2009) and the DNA binding dissociation constant (Kd-binding) of FEN1 and NonEQ DF-6,1 as determined by surface plasmon resonance (SPR) (Figure 1—figure supplement 4B).
evidence: This is supported by comparison with bulk assay data and SPR measurements shown in supplement figures.

claim: FEN1 actively bent EQ DF-6,1dsDNA to a similar extent and similar Kd-bending as DF-NonEQ 6,1dsDNA.
source: To mimic the in vivo junction, we used equilibrated (EQ) DF-6,1 (Figure 1A). FEN1 actively bent EQ DF-6,1dsDNA to a similar extent and similar Kd-bending as DF-NonEQ 6,1dsDNA (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B,C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data shown in the supplement figures.

claim: Time traces of EQ DF-6,1 showed multiple transitions between bent and unbent states.
source: Nonetheless, time traces showed multiple transitions between bent and unbent states (Figure 1G).
evidence: This is directly shown in the single-molecule time traces in Figure 1G.

claim: The second-order association rate constant (kon-bending) for FEN1 bending EQ DF-6,1 was diffusion-limited (1.4 ± 0.03×10^8 M^-1 s^-1).
source: Notably, the second-order association rate constant (kon-bending) calculated from the slope of the linear fit of the concentration dependence of kbending was diffusion-limited (1.4 ± 0.03×108 M−1 s−1), and the average value of kunbending (koff-unbending) was 0.45 ± 0.05 s−1 (Figure 1G).
evidence: This is calculated from dwell time analysis shown in Figure 1G.

claim: EXO1 actively bent a DNA nick with diffusion-limited kon-bending.
source: To see if active bending of the ss/ds-DNA junction may be a conserved feature in 5'nucleases, we tested human mismatch repair exonuclease 1 (EXO1), which recognizes an ideal junction of either a nick or a 3' overhang (Orans et al., 2011). EXO1 actively bent a DNA nick with diffusion-limited kon-bending (Figure 1H); the donor and acceptor had identical positions to those in NonEQ DF-6,1dsDNA.
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data shown in Figure 1H.

claim: FEN1 always bent NonEQ DF-6,1Flap before cleaving the Cy3-containing 5'flap.
source: Time traces indicated that FEN1 always bent NonEQ DF-6,1Flap before cleaving the Cy3-containing 5'flap; remarkably every DNA bending event led to a successful cleavage reaction (Figure 2A, Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is directly demonstrated by single-molecule cleavage time traces shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Every DNA bending event led to a successful cleavage reaction for the cognate substrate.
source: Time traces indicated that FEN1 always bent NonEQ DF-6,1Flap before cleaving the Cy3-containing 5'flap; remarkably every DNA bending event led to a successful cleavage reaction (Figure 2A, Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is directly demonstrated by single-molecule cleavage experiments shown in Figure 2A.

claim: FEN1 cleaved NonEQ DF-6,1Flap from a fully bent state.
source: Analysis of FRET values before cleavage from individual time traces showed that FEN1 cleaved NonEQ DF-6,1Flap from a fully bent state (Figure 2B) and remained bent for 160 ± 7 ms prior to cleavage (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by analysis of FRET values before cleavage shown in Figure 2B.

claim: FEN1 remained bent for 160 ± 7 ms prior to cleavage.
source: Analysis of FRET values before cleavage from individual time traces showed that FEN1 cleaved NonEQ DF-6,1Flap from a fully bent state (Figure 2B) and remained bent for 160 ± 7 ms prior to cleavage (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is calculated from dwell time analysis shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The single turnover kcat (kSTO) was 6.3 ± 0.2 s^-1.
source: Notably, our kSTO (6.3 ± 0.2 s−1) was comparable to that determined by bulk cleavage assays (kSTO 12.3 s−1−>5 s−1) (Algasaier et al., 2016; Stodola and Burgers, 2016), with the slight difference explained by the lower reaction temperature in the single molecule assays.
evidence: This is calculated from single-molecule cleavage dwell times and compared to bulk assay data.

claim: The diffusion-limited rates of DNA bending and cleavage before protein dissociation provide direct evidence that the reaction of FEN1 on a cognate substrate is limited by encounters between the enzyme and the substrate.
source: The diffusion-limited rates of DNA bending and cleavage before protein dissociation provide direct evidence that the reaction of FEN1 on a cognate substrate is limited by encounters between the enzyme and the substrate.
evidence: This is inferred from the measured diffusion-limited kon-bending and the observation that every bending leads to cleavage.

claim: Increasing glycerol concentration decreased kSTO linearly with a slope of 1.5 ± 0.2.
source: To test this idea, we employed glycerol and sucrose as low-molecular-weight viscogen to slow any local protein conformational change that mediates catalysis and/or product release. Increasing glycerol concentration decreased kSTO linearly with a slope of 1.5 ± 0.2 (Figure 2D and Figure 2—figure supplement 1B); a similar effect was observed with sucrose (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by viscosity experiments shown in Figure 2D.

claim: kSTO was unaffected by polyethylene glycol-8000, a high-molecular-weight viscogen.
source: Yet, kSTO was unaffected by polyethylene glycol-8000, a high-molecular-weight viscogen that is too large to interfere with local protein conformational changes (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by control experiments shown in the supplement figure.

claim: The cleavage behavior from the first DNA bending and the kSTO were similar whether there was a deliberate mispaired 3'flap (NonEQ DF-6,1) or an equilibrating 3'flap (EQ DF-6,1).
source: Biologically relevant, the cleavage behavior from the first DNA bending and the kSTO were similar whether there was a deliberate mispaired 3'flap (NonEQ DF-6,1; Figure 2A,C and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A) or an equilibrating 3'flap (EQ DF-6,1; Figure 2E,F and Figure 2—figure supplement 1E), consistent with bulk cleavage reactions (Tarantino et al., 2015).
evidence: This is demonstrated by comparison of cleavage data for both substrates and supported by citation.

claim: FEN1 actively bent SF-6,0 substrate.
source: Time traces on surface-immobilized SF-6,0Flap accessed at 5 ms using confocal-based smFRET showed that FEN1 actively bent SF (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is directly shown by single-molecule time traces in Figure 3A.

claim: The τbending of SF-6,0 was markedly reduced to ~43 ms (koff-unbending = 23.3 ± 3.8 s^-1) in contrast to that of the stable bent conformer in NonEQ DF-6,1.
source: The τbending was markedly reduced to ~43 ms (koff-unbending = 23.3 ± 3.8 s−1) in contrast to that of the stable bent conformer in NonEQ DF-6,1 (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is calculated from dwell time analysis shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The kon-bending of SF-6,0 remained limited by diffusion and similar to that of EQ DF-6,1dsDNA.
source: However, the kon-bending remained limited by diffusion and similar to that of EQ DF-6,1dsDNA (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is shown by kinetic analysis in Figure 3A.

claim: Kd-bending of SF-6,0 was 50-fold higher than for NonEQ DF-6,1.
source: Kd-bending was 50-fold higher than for NonEQ DF-6,1 (Figure 3A), consistent with that observed from confocal-based smFRET with burst analysis of freely diffusing SF-6,0dsDNA (Figure 1—figure supplement 4D) and the markedly increased Kd-binding by SPR (Figure 1—figure supplement 4B).
evidence: This is calculated from binding data and confirmed by multiple methods shown in the figures.

claim: A 3'flap is not required for DNA bending but it is critical for DNA binding stability.
source: These results show that a 3'flap is not required for DNA bending but it is critical for DNA binding stability.
evidence: This is inferred from the comparison of bending kinetics between DF and SF substrates.

claim: The FRET values of the substrate alone in EQ DF-6,1dsDNA and in SF-6,0dsDNA were similar (E ~ 0.27), but less than that in NonEQ DF-6,1dsDNA (E ~ 0.34).
source: Interestingly, we found that the FRET values of the substrate alone in EQ DF-6,1dsDNA and in SF-6,0dsDNA were similar (E ~ 0.27), but less than that in NonEQ DF-6,1dsDNA (E ~ 0.34) (Figure 3B; Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is measured from FRET histograms shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The equilibrated junction existed as a SF.
source: This suggests that the equilibrated junction existed as a SF, which was shown by free MD simulations not to equilibrate to a DF (Figure 1—figure supplement 3D,E).
evidence: This is inferred from FRET measurements and supported by MD simulations.

claim: FEN1 actively converts the equilibrated junction from a SF to a DF by pulling out its 3'end to create a 3'flap.
source: The finding that FEN1 cleaves equilibrated and non-equilibrated DF substrates with equal activity (Tarantino et al., 2015) prompted us to propose that FEN1 actively converts the equilibrated junction from a SF to a DF by pulling out its 3'end to create a 3'flap.
evidence: This is inferred from FRET measurements showing junction movement and supported by citation.

claim: The bent conformer in EQ DF-6,1dsDNA had identical FRET to that in NonEQ DF-6,1 (E ~ 0.54).
source: The bent conformer in EQ DF-6,1dsDNA had identical FRET to that in NonEQ DF-6,1 (E ~ 0.54) (Figure 3B; Figure 3—figure supplement 1), demonstrating that the equilibrated nick junction must have moved by one base pair.
evidence: This is measured from FRET histograms shown in Figure 3B.

claim: FEN1 actively sculpts the 3'end of its in vivo equilibrated nick junction to create a 3'flap and to drive its ordering.
source: These data therefore suggest that FEN1 actively sculpts the 3'end of its in vivo equilibrated nick junction to create a 3'flap and to drive its ordering.
evidence: This is inferred from the FRET data showing junction movement in equilibrated substrate.

claim: The FRET value of the bent conformer in SF-6,0dsDNA was similar to that of NonEQ DF-6,1dsDNA.
source: We found that the FRET value of the bent conformer in SF-6,0dsDNA was also similar to that of NonEQ DF-6,1dsDNA (Figure 3B; Figure 3—figure supplement 1), demonstrating that the nick junction must have moved by one base pair.
evidence: This is measured from FRET histograms shown in Figure 3B.

claim: FEN1 creates 3'flaps at noncognate nick junctions.
source: This indicates that FEN1 creates 3'flaps at noncognate nick junctions, suggesting that there is another requirement during substrate validation.
evidence: This is inferred from the FRET data showing junction movement in SF substrate.

claim: The Kd-bending of DF-6,1 containing a one-nucleotide mismatch at the junction increased by seven fold.
source: Here, the Kd-bending of DF-6,1 containing a one-nucleotide mismatch at the junction (termed DF-7,1mismatch(1nt)-Flap) increased by seven fold (Figure 4A), with the time traces showing a less-stable bent conformer (Figure 4B and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is measured from binding experiments shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Only the junctions that are fully paired are stably bent.
source: Since FEN1 forms 3'flaps for both cognate and noncognate substrates, only the junctions that are fully paired are therefore stably bent.
evidence: This is inferred from the comparison of bending stability between matched and mismatched junctions.

claim: R47 in the hydrophobic wedge stacks against the first base pair on the 3'flap side of the junction while its side chain C-caps the α2 in the gateway and stacks with K128 on α5 in the cap.
source: The superfamily semi-conserved R47 in the hydrophobic wedge is poised to mediate this coordination: it stacks against the first base pair on the 3'flap side of the junction while its side chain C-caps the α2 in the gateway and stacks with K128 on α5 in the cap (Tsutakawa et al., 2011) (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is based on structural analysis cited and shown in Figure 4C.

claim: FEN1-R47A on NonEQ DF-6,1dsDNA showed defects in Kd-bending and koff-unbending that resemble those in wt-FEN1 on SF-6,0.
source: To test this allosteric signaling idea, we maintained the 3'flap binding using NonEQ DF-6,1dsDNA while altering R47 using FEN1-R47A. The defects in Kd-bending and koff-unbending resemble those in wt-FEN1 on SF-6,0 (Figure 4A,B and Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by comparison of mutant and wild-type data shown in Figure 4A,B.

claim: Blocking the threading by immobilizing a DF substrate through a biotin attached at the end of a 30 nt ssDNA 5'flap impaired DNA bending to comparable Kd-bending and koff-unbending of SF-6,0.
source: To test possible threading and its coordination with the 3'flap-induced protein ordering, we used a modification that prevented 5'flap threading. Blocking the threading by immobilizing a DF substrate through a biotin attached at the end of a 30 nt ssDNA 5'flap (termed DF-30,1blocked-dsDNA) impaired DNA bending to comparable Kd-bending and koff-unbending of SF-6,0 (Figure 4A,B and Figure 4—figure supplement 1C), consistent with the markedly reduced Kd-binding captured by SPR (Figure 1—figure supplement 4B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by experiments with blocked threading shown in Figure 4A,B.

claim: Initial DNA bending by FEN1 did not require threading, but full bending required 5'flaps, if present, to be able to thread.
source: This significant DNA distortion was masked in our previous experiment that relied on a flap labeling scheme to infer to the geometry of the blocked-threaded complex (Sobhy et al., 2013). Importantly, our new results indicate that initial DNA bending by FEN1 did not require threading, but that full bending required 5'flaps, if present, to be able to thread.
evidence: This is inferred from comparison of bent FRET states with and without threading block.

claim: The increased Kd-bending of the unthreaded substrate upon removal of its 3'flap indicates that 3'flap binding did not require 5'flap threading.
source: The increased Kd-bending of the unthreaded substrate upon removal of its 3'flap (SF-30,0blocked-dsDNA) (Figure 4A) indicates that 3'flap binding did not require 5'flap threading.
evidence: This is inferred from comparison of binding data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The ability of the 5'flap to thread is required for the 3'flap-induced protein ordering to form the stably and correctly bent DNA conformer.
source: However, the ability of the 5'flap to thread is required for the 3'flap-induced protein ordering to form the stably and correctly bent DNA conformer.
evidence: This is inferred from the comparison of bending stability with and without threading capability.

claim: FEN1 bends both cognate and noncognate substrates and Kd-bending is higher for noncognate substrates.
source: Collectively, these results demonstrate that FEN1 bends both cognate and noncognate substrates and that Kd-bending is higher for noncognate substrates.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion from the binding data comparing different substrates.

claim: In SF-6,0, the lifetime of the bent conformer was ~3.5 fold shorter than the required lag time prior to cleaving the cognate substrate.
source: To test the mechanism for assembly of catalytically competent active sites for cognate substrate incision, we compared the lifetime of the bent conformer to the lag time for cleaving correct versus incorrect substrates. In SF-6,0, the lifetime of the bent conformer was ~3.5 fold shorter than the required lag time prior to cleaving the cognate substrate (Figure 3A and Figure 2C).
evidence: This is calculated by comparing data from Figure 3A and Figure 2C.

claim: SF-6,0 underwent multiple cycles of DNA bending and unbending before a successful DNA bending event led to 5'flap cleavage.
source: Traces of single-molecule cleavage showed that SF-6,0 underwent multiple cycles of DNA bending and unbending before a successful DNA bending event led to 5'flap cleavage (Figure 5A; Figure 5—figure supplement 1A; Figure 2—figure supplement 2E).
evidence: This is directly shown by single-molecule cleavage traces in Figure 5A.

claim: Destabilizing the bent DNA intermediate to rates that are limiting for catalysis reduces the probability of assembling catalytically competent active sites.
source: These results show that destabilizing the bent DNA intermediate to rates that are limiting for catalysis reduces the probability of assembling catalytically competent active sites.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that substrates with shorter bent lifetimes require multiple bending attempts before cleavage.

claim: DF-7,1mismatch(1nt)-Flap and DF-6,2Flap exhibited koff-unbending that was ~13–15 fold slower than that of SF-6,0 and ~3–4 fold longer than kSTO of the cognate substrate.
source: Interestingly, we also observed similar bending behavior without cleavage of FEN1 on noncognate substrates under conditions in which the lifetime of the bent conformer does not limit catalysis. DF-7,1mismatch(1nt)-Flap and DF containing 2 nt 3'flap (DF-6,2Flap) exhibited koff-unbending that was ~13–15 fold slower than that of SF-6,0 and ~3–4 fold longer than kSTO of the cognate substrate (Figure 4B and Figure 2C), yet FEN1 still bent these substrates multiple times without cleaving them (Figure 5C,D and Figure 5—figure supplement 1C,D).
evidence: This is calculated from kinetic data shown in Figure 4B and Figure 2C.

claim: FEN1 likely has intrinsic mechanisms that block the probable formation of catalytically competent active sites in noncognate substrates to inhibit off-target incision.
source: FEN1 therefore likely has intrinsic mechanisms that block the probable formation of catalytically competent active sites in noncognate substrates to inhibit off-target incision.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that noncognate substrates with long bent lifetimes still undergo multiple bending cycles without cleavage.

claim: The kSTO of FEN1 in all tested noncognate substrates was similar and comparable to that in the cognate substrate.
source: We found that the kSTO of FEN1 in all tested noncognate substrates was similar and comparable to that in the cognate substrate (Figure 5A–D and Figure 2C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by comparison of cleavage dwell times across different substrates.

claim: The 3'flap-induced protein ordering locked the DNA into either a catalytically competent conformation to be immediately incised or into an incompetent conformation that led to immediate DNA release from the bent conformation.
source: This indicates that the 3'flap-induced protein ordering locked the DNA into either a catalytically competent conformation to be immediately incised or into an incompetent conformation that led to immediate DNA release from the bent conformation.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that kSTO is similar across substrates despite different numbers of bending attempts.

claim: Mutating individual gateway residues Y40, K93, R100 or D181 to alanine markedly reduced the bent conformer's stability.
source: Given that FEN1 actively bends the DNA, it is unclear how FEN1 positions the junction before it locks down the DNA conformation. We therefore tested the role of key active-site residues. Mutating individual gateway residues Y40, K93, R100 or one of the metal-coordinating aspartic acidic residues (D181) to alanine markedly reduced the bent conformer's stability (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is demonstrated by mutational analysis shown in Figure 6A.

claim: kon-bending was reduced up to 11 fold in gateway mutants, with R100 and to a lesser extent Y40 being critical residues.
source: Interestingly, kon-bending was reduced up to 11 fold in gateway mutants, with R100 and to a lesser extent Y40 being critical residues (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by kinetic analysis of mutants shown in Figure 6B.

claim: D181A had only a minor effect on kon-bending, implying that the metal ions do not interact with the phosphates during DNA bending and 5'flap threading.
source: Moreover, D181A had only a minor effect on kon-bending, implying that the metal ions do not interact with the phosphates during DNA bending and 5'flap threading.
evidence: This is inferred from the mutational analysis of the metal-coordinating residue.

claim: FEN1-Y40A cleaves DF-6,1 after multiple cycles of DNA bending and unbending.
source: FEN1-Y40A is the only active-site mutation that retains activity, albeit with a 100-fold reduced kSTO (Algasaier et al., 2016). Y40 is proposed to play various roles in substrate positioning, including placing FEN1 at the junction, at the 5'flap in the cap-helical gateway and at the scissile phosphate in the active site (Algasaier et al., 2016; Tsutakawa et al., 2011). We observed that FEN1-Y40A cleaves DF-6,1 after multiple cycles of DNA bending and unbending (Figure 6C, Figure 5—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This is demonstrated by single-molecule cleavage traces shown in Figure 6C.

claim: The kSTO in FEN1-Y40A increased by about three fold compared to wild-type.
source: Unlike noncognate substrates or FEN1-R47A, the kSTO in FEN1-Y40A increased by about three fold (Figure 6C); nonetheless, koff-unbending was still about two-fold slower than its kSTO (Figure 6A,C).
evidence: This is calculated from cleavage dwell time analysis shown in Figure 6C.

claim: There is another step after proper DNA lockdown that involves active positioning of the scissile phosphate for incision.
source: This indicates the presence of another step after proper DNA lockdown that involves active positioning of the scissile phosphate for incision.
evidence: This is inferred from the Y40A mutant data showing increased kSTO despite proper DNA lockdown.
